sections.theory:
Introduction

Some important classes of organic compounds like aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amides, acid halides and acid anhydrides contain a group called carbonyl group (shown below), and are therefore called carbonyl compounds. Many of these compounds are important commercially and in biological processes. In addition to their uses as reagents and solvents, they are constituents of fabrics, flavorings, plastics, and drugs. Naturally occurring carbonyl compounds include proteins, carbohydrates and nucleic acids which constitute major portion of plants and animals body.

A carbonyl group is a functional group which is composed of a carbon atom doubly bonded to an oxygen atom.

The simplest carbonyl compounds are ketones and aldehydes. A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon atom. An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom bonded to the carbonyl carbon atom. The functional group of aldehyde, which is carbonyl group along with one hydrogen (–CHO), is also called formyl group. Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde, with two hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbonyl group.

If the two alkyl groups attached to carbonyl carbon are the same the ketone is called symmetrical and if different, it is called unsymmetrical ketone. Instead of alkyl, aryl group(s) can also be attached to carbonyl carbon, in aromatic aldehydes and ketones.

19.1 Nomenclature

Two types of naming systems are used for naming aldehydes and ketones. Common system and IUPAC system.

19.1.1 Nomenclature of Aldehydes

a. Common System

Common names of aldehydes are derived from the common names of carboxylic acids containing the same number of carbon atoms (Section 20.1). While naming aldehydes in this system, the ending “-ic acid” in the common name of corresponding carboxylic acid is replaced by the word “-aldehyde”.

The position of other groups on the chain are indicated by Greek letters, α, β, γ etc. Letter starts from the carbon atom adjacent to formyl group. The first letter, is given to the carbon atom next to the carbonyl group.

b. IUPAC System

In this system, following rules are used for naming aldehydes.

1. In IUPAC system, the ending “–e” of the corresponding alkane is replaced by “–al”.

2. Prefixes di–, tri– etc. is added before suffix –al, when two or three carbonyl groups respectively, are present.

3. If the aldehyde group is attached to a ring, the suffix carbaldehyde is used.

4. Locate the longest chain of carbon atoms containing formyl group to get the stem name.

5. Carbon atoms of the selected chain are numbered from the carbon of formyl group (–CHO) because it is always at the terminal position. It is not necessary to mention the position of aldehydic carbonyl.

6. The rules for naming substituents are same as in case of alkanes.

Introduction

Some important classes of organic compounds like aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amides, acid halides and acid anhydrides contain a group called carbonyl group (shown below), and are therefore called carbonyl compounds. Many of these compounds are important commercially and in biological processes. In addition to their uses as reagents and solvents, they are constituents of fabrics, flavorings, plastics, and drugs. Naturally occurring carbonyl compounds include proteins, carbohydrates and nucleic acids which constitute major portion of plants and animals body.

A carbonyl group is a functional group which is composed of a carbon atom doubly bonded to an oxygen atom.

The simplest carbonyl compounds are ketones and aldehydes. A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon atom. An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom bonded to the carbonyl carbon atom. The functional group of aldehyde, which is carbonyl group along with one hydrogen (–CHO), is also called formyl group. Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde, with two hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbonyl group.

If the two alkyl groups attached to carbonyl carbon are the same the ketone is called symmetrical and if different, it is called unsymmetrical ketone. Instead of alkyl, aryl group(s) can also be attached to carbonyl carbon, in aromatic aldehydes and ketones.

19.1 Nomenclature

Two types of naming systems are used for naming aldehydes and ketones. Common system and IUPAC system.

19.1.1 Nomenclature of Aldehydes

a. Common System

Common names of aldehydes are derived from the common names of carboxylic acids containing the same number of carbon atoms (Section 20.1). While naming aldehydes in this system, the ending “-ic acid” in the common name of corresponding carboxylic acid is replaced by the word “-aldehyde”.

The position of other groups on the chain are indicated by Greek letters, α, β, γ etc. Letter starts from the carbon atom adjacent to formyl group. The first letter, is given to the carbon atom next to the carbonyl group.

b. IUPAC System

In this system, following rules are used for naming aldehydes.

1. In IUPAC system, the ending “–e” of the corresponding alkane is replaced by “–al”.

2. Prefixes di–, tri– etc. is added before suffix –al, when two or three carbonyl groups respectively, are present.

3. If the aldehyde group is attached to a ring, the suffix carbaldehyde is used.

4. Locate the longest chain of carbon atoms containing formyl group to get the stem name.

5. Carbon atoms of the selected chain are numbered from the carbon of formyl group (–CHO) because it is always at the terminal position. It is not necessary to mention the position of aldehydic carbonyl.
